title: As LIV Golf 2.0 deadline arrives, 1 big question holds answer to league's future
article_text:
Back in April, as rumors swirled that the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund (PIF) was set to withdraw funding from LIV Golf, Bryson DeChambeau pledged his fealty to the future of a league that wasn’t guaranteed to have one.

“As long as LIV is here, I would figure out a way for it to make sense,” DeChambeau told the social media account Flushing It days before the PIF officially withdrew funding.

A few months later, as LIV’s season ended early and the prospects of LIV 2.0 remained murky, DeChambeau again assumed his role as LIV’s biggest advocate.

“I think there’s a lot of potential moving forward. It’s been an interesting ride, that’s for sure,” DeChambeau said. “Everything that we’ve gone through and the tough moments that we’ve had. But it’s made us stronger. … As much as we’re transitioning from LIV 1.0 to 2.0, I have great thoughts about what could happen next year. I wish I could be more up front about it.”

Ever the showman looking to draw attention, DeChambeau then spoke about LIV in the past tense even as he supposedly looked to a future with the league post-Saudi exit.

“If there’s one thing that I could say, it’s we did something different in the game of golf, and I’m proud of that,” DeChambeau said.

That was the last time DeChambeau spoke publicly about LIV’s future. Since then, the league has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, secured an initial targeted investment for LIV 2.0 from BC Partners Global, and seen numerous players, including Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton, exit the league. The list of players who have said “thanks but no thanks” to LIV 2.0 is much longer than the one of players who have signed back up. You can count those on one hand: Ben Campbell, Cameron Tringale, Richard Bland and Brendan Steele. In the other column, Rahm, Hatton, Ian Poulter, David Puig, Adrian Meronk, Tom McKibbin, Louis Oosthuizen and Abraham Ancer are among those who have confirmed that they are departing LIV Golf.

But we don’t yet have the full picture, which is why Sunday is a marquee date for LIV Golf and its future prospects.

The restructuring support agreement (RSA) between BC Partners and LIV Golf that was filed with the courts moved back the deadline for players to commit to LIV 2.0 to Oct. 25. But the RSA also gave BC Partners full autonomy to decide whether LIV has earned enough player commitments to do business. LIV’s lawyers have said they will know by the end of October whether LIV 2.0 is a go or if they are closing up shop, but Sunday’s commitment deadline is expected to be a “soft” deadline as BC Partners and LIV Golf try to secure enough talent to get LIV 2.0 off the ground.

That starts and ends with DeChambeau, who by all accounts has been working behind the scenes to help get LIV 2.0 up and running. LIV Golf CEO Scott O’Neil has said that DeChambeau is even more “pro-LIV” than he is. Everything we’ve seen and heard from DeChambeau over the past four years would suggest that’s true. While Phil Mickelson got LIV off the ground and Dustin Johnson helped give it legitimacy at the outset, it’s DeChambeau who has been its biggest cheerleader and supporter. The league and his growing YouTube audience gave him popularity he couldn’t find on the PGA Tour. That was on display at the 2024 U.S. Open, where he was the Pinehurst crowd favorite in a battle with Rory McIlroy. LIV Golf has been good to Bryson DeChambeau.

But now, as the LIV 2.0 deadline arrives, we’re going to get the answer to the question that will determine the league’s fate. What really matters to Bryson DeChambeau?

With the mass exodus of talent, LIV 2.0, if it comes to fruition, would include DeChambeau and a roster of players of far lower wattage and world ranking than the one the PIF-backed operation put together with billions of dollars in a soft-power exercise at its inception. It would be the DeChambeau show for 10 tournaments a year, and he could spend the rest of his time building his YouTube channel and trying to stay sharp for the majors despite a lack of major tour. That would make him the star attraction for 10 weeks a year — the sun a league revolves around — and give him time to focus on new challenges and new subscribers most of the year.

If that’s what Bryson DeChambeau wants, then he’ll continue being the frontman for Crushers GC, with whatever teammates he can cobble together, and then show up at four tournaments that really matter and see if he can render the idea of “competitive reps” meaningless. But if the two-time major champion who loved and idolized Arnold Palmer truly cares, as he says, about the game’s trajectory, its growth and his own legacy, then he’ll follow Rahm and others out the door and see what his competitive future holds post-LIV. He’ll come hat in hand to the established tours — though also with the knowledge of what he brings to their business — be willing to pay a penalty, and then rejoin the ecosystem.

“The reality is I’m so focused on what I can do for the game that somebody saying something online or to me personally in my face is not going to distract me from the mission that I have,” DeChambeau said in LIV Golf Korea. “I hope people can understand that, that my goal is bigger than just winning every tournament every single week. Do I want to win every week? 100 percent. Do I care about the game sometimes more than my own life? Yeah. Because I see what it can do for people’s lives. That’s ultimately why I care so much and I’m so passionate and I want the best for everybody.”

title: What Cameron Young said about Brooks Koepka returning as it’s revealed he agreed to join LIV himself
article_text:
One of the more intriguing pieces of news to emerge from LIV Golf’s bankruptcy hearings in recent days concerned Cameron Young.

Cameron Young is now one of the best players on the PGA Tour, having won The Players Championship and finished in the top-three at two of the four majors in 2026. However, history could have been very different for the 29-year-old.

Which player do you expect to benefit most from leaving LIV Golf?

Several names have already announced they will not be involved with LIV 2.0

It was revealed this week that Young had actually reached an agreement with LIV Golf to join the league back in 2022, one week after finishing second to Cam Smith at The Open Championship.

It is not clear what convinced Young to stay with the PGA Tour. He did play in the Presidents Cup later that year, but he would have to wait another three years to win on the PGA Tour for the very first time.

Young would have almost certainly not been the only player to agree a deal with LIV before backing out. But his decision does make his perspective on what happens next much more interesting.

Of course, the PGA Tour welcomed Brooks Koepka back earlier this year. Meanwhile, there has been speculation throughout the season concerning the future of LIV.

Speaking to ESPN back in May, Young was asked about having Koepka back, as well as the possibility of more LIV players returning in the future.

“I feel like it’s a little bit tricky. I think it’s been great to have Brooks back. He’s a fan favourite, he’s a great golfer, great major championship player, so I’m happy to have him back. I think it’s good for the PGA Tour, I think it’s good for the game to get to see him more. The tour did have the system that they put in place for him. They had the opportunity this January for some of those guys, the select few, to come back, and Brooks was the only one to take that opportunity,” he said.

“It’s not up to me, but I think the PGA Tour, I imagine they’ll find a way for some of those guys to come back, but I don’t know if it will be as simple as it was for Brooks. Time-wise, he didn’t have to sit out or anything like that, so I really have no good information on what will happen, but all in all I play golf to play golf against the best players in the world. That’s one of the main things that drives me is to compete. To me, there’s a handful of really, really good players that are over there, and seeing them four times a year I probably would rather compete against them more.

“If you’re asking me, I’d probably like to see them back in some capacity however they decide it’s going to work out. And you’d like it to be fair to both sides, I don’t think there’s any reason to unduly punish them coming back. But at the same time, it felt like an all or nothing decision to go. It’s up to people smarter than me to figure it all out.”

Obviously, Young’s trajectory would have been completely different had he decided to go through with signing with LIV back in 2022.

He may well have had more immediate success when you consider that he did not win on the PGA Tour until 2025. However, Young must be delighted with where he is right now, with a major championship victory surely the next step in his career.

He has top-five finishes at each of the four majors across his career. Meanwhile, he was a star at both the 2025 Ryder Cup and the Presidents Cup in September.

In hindsight, signing with LIV appeared to put a much lower ceiling on a lot of players. Very few will leave with evidence to show that they are better players than when they joined, though their bank balances should certainly soften the blow.

Had Young made the jump, he may well have won much sooner. But he will surely reflect now that he made the right decision when he chose to stay with the PGA Tour.

title: Which players earned their DP World Tour cards for 2027? Full Race to Dubai Rankings
article_text:
Sean Crocker produced a clutch final round at the Genesis Championship to secure a crucial DP World Tour lifeline for 2027, prompting a warm message of congratulations from fellow professional Eddie Pepperell.

The American carded a closing 68 at Woo Jeong Hills Country Club in South Korea, finishing at 4-under par after a superb back nine of 29. That late charge lifted Crocker to 100th in the Race to Dubai Rankings with 534.64 points — the provisional cut-off for retaining DP World Tour Category 10 status.

It was a significant moment for the 30-year-old, who was visibly emotional when speaking to Sky Sports Golf after his round.

A former DP World Tour winner, Crocker knew what was at stake and delivered when it mattered most.

Pepperell, who finished 101st on 518.18 points, was among those quick to recognise the achievement.

The 35-year-old Englishman ended the season just 16.46 points behind Crocker, but his own hopes of retaining the same level of playing status were left hanging in the balance.

In a message on X, Pepperell wrote: “Now, Sean Crocker, that is how you do it.”

He added: “Big balls, minerals you could say. Very well done. You can buy me a bourbon when I next see you.”

Pepperell’s season is not necessarily over in terms of opportunity, with his 101st-place finish still set to provide him with a number of DP World Tour starts next season.

However, Crocker’s late surge underlined just how fine the margins can be when players are fighting to preserve their status.

One of the week’s more difficult stories involved Pablo Larrazábal, the nine-time DP World Tour winner who arrived at the Genesis Championship needing a runner-up finish to have a chance of extending his remarkable run on the circuit to a 20th consecutive season.

The 43-year-old Spaniard missed the cut, bringing a frustrating campaign to a close after nine consecutive missed cuts.

“Well very, very, very tough,” Larrazábal said. “Yeah, just a very tough moment. I had to play my worst golf the season that I had to keep my card.”

His comments captured the pressure of the season-ending battle, where even players with long and successful Tour careers can find themselves fighting for their future.

At the top of the leaderboard, Japan’s Yuto Katsuragawa won the Genesis Championship after a final-round 71 took him to 13-under par.

It was his second DP World Tour title, arriving two years and 180 days after his first victory at the ISPS HANDA Championship.

The win lifted Katsuragawa 78 places to 28th in the Race to Dubai Rankings, with 1,296.13 points.

Martin Couvra and Frederic Lacroix shared second place on 11-under par. Couvra climbed 39 places to 27th with 1,297.68 points, while Lacroix rose 36 places to 42nd on 1,166.97.

Attention now turns to the DP World Tour Play-Offs in Abu Dhabi and Dubai next month, where the top 10 eligible players in the Race to Dubai will secure PGA Tour cards for the 2027 season.

Eugenio Chacarra currently leads that race, ahead of Patrick Reed and Casey Jarvis.

The second stage of DP World Tour Q School starts next week.

At Final Stage, 15 players will earn DP World Tour cards for 2027 — down from the 20 cards available last year.

With playing status, career opportunities and major financial implications at stake, the closing stretch of the season promises plenty more drama.

Scroll down to see how the race for the 10 PGA Tour cards stands heading into next month's Playoffs.

Scroll down for a look at the final regular season standings on the 2026 DP World Tour, with the top 100 earning their full playing rights for 2027.

The top 70 on the rankings advance to the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, with the top 50 after that qualifying for the season-ending DP World Tour Championship where the leader in the standings following the final round will be crowned Race to Dubai champion for 2026.

title: Bristol overcome Exeter to go third in Prem
article_text:
Bristol moved up to third place in the Prem after beating Exeter 20-7 at Ashton Gate.

Gabriel Ibitoye's 26th-minute try and James Williams' penalty three minutes later were the only scores of an attritional first half in difficult conditions.

Greg Fisilau was mauled over 12 minutes after the restart as Exeter got on the scoreboard.

The Chiefs tried to force a second, but it was Bristol that earned the win when Williams kicked an excellent 41-metre penalty before Luca Ivanishvili crashed over from close range after Olly Woodburn had fumbled a high ball.

His late try denied Exeter a losing bonus point and leaves Rob Baxter's side in ninth place on eight points, six behind the Bears.

The stormy weather's impact was in evidence from the first whistle as both sides struggled to keep hold of the ball.

Bristol almost scored in the opening 60 seconds after an Exeter mistake under a kick saw the ball bobble around in their in-goal area.

It was as close as either side came to scoring in the opening 26 minutes as the hosts had the better of the possession and territory but were stifled by a spirited Exeter defence.

The pressure finally told when Ibitoye got on the end of a looping Harry Randall pass and beat Zack Wimbush to dive into the left corner.

Williams' penalty soon after extended the lead to 10 points and Exeter then had Australia star Tom Hooper forced off with a shoulder injury just before the interval.

Despite that setback, Henry Slade almost dotted down a Sam Wolstenholme grubber kick four minutes after the restart before Exeter's maul got them back into the game soon after.

First the pack earned themselves a penalty and the second maul from the resulting lineout 10 metres out saw Fisilau forced over.

The Chiefs forwards won another penalty inside the 22 with eight minutes left, but superb work from Ibitoye saw the Bears turn the ball over six metres out.

Bristol went straight up the field and a penalty resulting from a high tackle was dispatched well by Williams despite the tough conditions.

And the weather proved to be a distraction for Woodburn soon after as he missed a high kick and was put under pressure by Ibitoye, who was stopped inches from the Exeter line.

But eight phases later Georgian replacement Ivanishvili forced his way over to seal a hard-fought victory.

"I'm really proud of the boys. We did what we needed to do to win, I felt.

"Some might say it's not pretty, but it's the type of rugby that needed to be played in these conditions.

"We knew earlier in the week it was going to be like this, so we just shone the light on this part of the game that we don't always use.

"This was the part of the game that we had to use, so I'm really pleased the boys got their rewards for it."

"I thought towards the end there we'd worked our way back into it and we had an opportunity to get something, didn't we?

"Obviously our poorest maul of the game probably was at the end point there when you probably needed to have a real killer maul at that stage.

"We weren't quite as good as we needed to be there, so we have to play away from it and then we lost the ball and then I think really that last period was the kind of errors you just can't afford to have in these conditions - not just handling errors but we gave away penalty error as well which gives a shot at goal.

"We did just make more errors than them over the course of today and tactically they were potentially a little smarter."

title: ATP Rankings: How many points will Sinner, Zverev, Alcaraz, Shelton, Djokovic drop next week?
article_text:
It is set to be a big week in the ATP Rankings for the week of 26 October as players will not only drop points from last year’s Vienna Open and Swiss Indoors, but also the Paris Masters.

The ATP uses a rolling 52-week, cumulative system to determine the ATP Rankings and it means players have to defend points from the corresponding tournament and/or period 12 months ago.

Points are removed in the Live ATP Rankings at the start of the current event and then players will earn points for their round-by-round progression.

The Vienna Open and Swiss Indoors are the two events on the calendar this coming week.

But just to add to the confusion, the Paris Masters took place a week earlier in 2026 so points that players earned from the ATP 1000 event will also be included in the points dropping total.

World No 1 Sinner, of course, won’t be in action this week as he was forced to end his 2026 season early due to his ongoing knee injury, but he could drop to No 2 in the rankings by the end of next week as he has the most to lose.

The Italian won the Vienna Open (500 points) and the Paris Masters (1,000) last year so 10,950 so he will drop to 9,450 points after the Vienna Open.

Zverev has a chance to become the new world No 1 on 2 November as he is only 880 points behind Sinner in the official rankings, while he will drop a total of 730 points.

The German finished runner-up (330) in Austria 12 months ago while he lost in the semi-final in Paris (400).

But even if he doesn’t finish the No 1 job in Vienna, he will get another chance in Paris.

The seven-time Grand Slam winner has a chance to chip away at the top two’s points lead as he will drop only 10 points, as he didn’t play Vienna or Basel last year and lost in the second round in Paris.

The American lost in the round of 16 in Basel (50) and was a quarter-finalist at the season-ending ATP Masters 1000 event in France.

Former world No 1 Medvedev is in the same boat as Shelton as he reached the round of 16 in Vienna (50) and the quarter-finals in Paris (200).

Deep runs in both of this year’s tournaments could help him to move clear of Cobolli and Auger-Aliassime in the rankings.

The world No 6 lost in the round of 16 in Vienna (50) and the round of 32 in Paris (50).

One of several players in the running for a place at ATP Finals, but Auger-Aliassime has the most points to defend from that group as he was a quarter-finalist in Basel (100) and finished runner-up to Sinner in Paris.

The Canadian is in danger of dropping out of the top 10.

The Australian was a semi-finalist in Vienna (200) and a quarter-finalist in Paris (200) last year and he too could drop down the rankings if he doesn’t perform well at the next two events.

Fils could boost his chances of qualifying for Turin this coming week as he doesn’t have any points to defend for the rest of the year after injury forced him to miss the final few months of the 2025 season.

Like Fils, Tiafoe also won’t drop any points and he could also boost his hopes of playing at the ATP Finals with a deep run in Vienna.

The Spaniard is currently 11th in the rankings and ninth in the Race To Turin.

Jodar, of course, was still playing lower-level events last year as he was ranked outside the top 200.

He will defend 75 points from his ATP Challenger Tour title run in Charlottesville 12 months ago.

The world No 12 has a big chance to move into the qualifying places for the ATP Finals as he didn’t play in Vienna, Basel or Paris last year.

Djokovic has signed up for the ATP 500 event in Switzerland next week and is also set to feature at the Paris Masters.

title: Novak Djokovic receives ATP Finals boost without playing as rivals suffer shock defeats
article_text:
Novak Djokovic’s Turin hopes received a boost after Arthur Fils’ shock loss to veteran Jan Lennard Struff in Brussels.

Fils was the top seed at the European Open, and after receiving a bye into the quarter-finals after Jaume Munar’s walkover, the Frenchman battled past Alex Michelsen in two tight sets in the last eight.

That set up an enticing semi-final clash with the big-hitting Struff, who was seeking the fifth ATP Tour final of his long career. The 36-year-old took the first set 6-4 but Fils battled back to claim the second on a tie-break on Saturday evening.

Although the Cincinnati Masters winner was the favourite to reach the final, where Tallon Griekspoor was waiting, the German held his nerve and claimed an impressive 6-4, 6-7 (9), 7-6 (5) victory in just under two hours and 20 minutes.

While Fils – who was broken when serving for the match at 5-4 in the decider – is up to a career high of eight, the 22-year-old missed the chance to put more daylight between him and his rivals in the race for the ATP Finals.

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

Following his win, world No 47 Struff said, “I want to thank the crowd for the support. It was an unreal match. I felt I played a very, very good first set, he won the second set which was very close. I managed to come back from a break down twice in the third set. I am just very happy to get the win.”

Despite this setback, Fils is still well placed to qualify for the season-ending event in Turin for the first time in his young career.

The Frenchman is seventh in the Race with 3,575 points, with Frances Tiafoe and Rafael Jodar making up the last two qualification spots on 3,380 and 3,159 points respectively.

24-time major winner Novak Djokovic is currently 11th in the Race on 2,840 points – exactly 319 points behind Jodar, who occupies the last qualification position.

Realistically, the Serbian is more likely to haul in Tiafoe or Jodar, but Fils’ defeat, along with Flavio Cobolli losing in three sets in Lyon to fellow Italian and world No 26 Lorenzo Musetti, means they will be looking over their shoulders nervously heading into Basel and Vienna.

Musetti won his quarter-final match after 1am this morning and had just over 12 hours to recover before taking on the French Open champion. Despite falling from world No 5 to outside the top 20 in an injury-hit season, the 24-year-old saved four match points and claimed a battling 4-6, 6-2, 7-5 victory.

For Djokovic, he may need to win either Basel or the Paris Masters, or at least have deep runs at both tournaments, to qualify for the ATP Finals.

Plus, Alex De Minaur and Lyon finalist Taylor Fritz will hope to crash the party in Turin. Incidentally, Daniil Medvedev sits in sixth but will jump to fifth if he wins the title in Almaty on Sunday.

Alexander Zverev has already been confirmed as the year-end No 1 due to Jannik Sinner’s season-ending knee injury, while Carlos Alcaraz and Ben Shelton have already qualified.

The qualification cut currently stands at 4,145 but that could change depending on how the remaining candidates do in the coming weeks.

title: 40 mph wind gusts suspend final round of Butterfield Bermuda Championship
article_text:
The final round of the 2026 Butterfield Bermuda Championship has been suspended due to high winds, and the PGA Tour has announced that players will not tee it up at all on Sunday.

With one round remaining, play was scheduled to begin early on Sunday morning with threesomes going off of split tees starting at 6:45 a.m. ET, despite a forecast of steady rain showers and wind.

But as the start time drew near on Sunday, tee times were first postponed by one hour to a 7:45 a.m. ET start, with the leaders in the final group scheduled to go off at 9:46 a.m. ET. But shortly after that update, the Tour called off the day’s play due to diminishing conditions and extremely high winds.

With one round remaining in Bermuda, two established players lead the field by two shots at 16 under par: Seamus Power, who won this tournament in 2022, and Austin Smotherman, who recently claimed his first career PGA Tour victory earlier this month at the Bank of Utah Championship.

Behind them are a multitude of players who are hoping to capitalize on a win or high finish at this point in the FedEx Cup Fall season. There are currently 14 players within four shots of the lead, including Tour veterans like Corey Connors and Chris Kirk.

title: Wallabies hopefuls push their cases after red card drama in USA
article_text:
Australia A overcame a red card to David Feliuai to thump the United States 61-12 in an impressive performance in Nashville on Sunday (AEDT).

Feliuai had started the match strongly at inside centre before getting yellow carded for a 15th minute high shot on Tavite Lopeti.

The TMO then upgraded it to red as Stephen Larkham’s side had to play 20 minutes with just 14 men.

It mattered not, as the Wallabies hopefuls furthered their cases for a call-up to the senior team that will play four Nations Championship Tests in November.

“What was pleasing from our perspective was when we had that red card for 20 minutes, and we were a man down,” Australia A captain Matt Faessler said on Stan Sport’s coverage.

“We really bit down on the mouthguard, worked for each other and ended up producing some points off the back of that, so it was very pleasing.

“We’re obviously a team that have only been together for a week or so now, but very close, a lot of us spend a fair bit of time with each other off the field, and I think that showed tonight.“

Faessler scored one of the visitors’ nine tries.

Winger Dylan Pietsch nabbed a double, while Nick Frost, Joe Brial, Nathan Hastie, Kadin Pritchard, Harry McLaughlin-Phillips and Tim Ryan also dotted down.

Queensland Reds No.8 Brial was named player of the match.

Australia A prop Tom Lambert and lock Miles Amatosero will now join the Wallabies camp in Sydney on Wednesday.

Australia A will take on the USA again in New Jersey on Saturday (AEDT).

Larkham is being assisted by former Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt.

title: England's dream route to 2027 Rugby World Cup final revealed – and it's VERY favourable
article_text:
England's potential route to the 2027 Rugby World Cup final has been mapped out, and Steve Borthwick's side could hardly have asked for a better opportunity.

The tournament kicks off in Australia next October, with England hoping to lift the Webb Ellis Cup for the first time since 2003.

And there is plenty of reason for optimism.

If England win their pool and the leading nations progress as expected, they could avoid South Africa, New Zealand and France until the final.

That's a huge incentive for Borthwick's men, who have been handed one of the more favourable draws among the leading contenders.

Of course, World Cups rarely follow the script. But on paper, England have a genuine chance to go all the way.

England begin their campaign against Tonga in Brisbane on 2 October before facing Zimbabwe in Adelaide six days later.

Borthwick's side face Wales in Sydney on 16 October, with top spot in Pool F potentially on the line.

England will be favourites to progress, but finishing first could make an enormous difference.

According to the official Rugby World Cup pool draw, England have avoided all five of the other top-seeded nations in the opening stage.

Should England top Pool F, they will face the runners-up from Pool B on 24 October in Perth.

That group contains South Africa, Italy, Georgia and Romania.

With the Springboks expected to finish first, Italy or Georgia could be waiting.

Neither should be underestimated, but England would fancy their chances against either opponent.

The expanded 24-team tournament also means Borthwick's side must negotiate four knockout matches rather than three.

This is where things could get interesting.

If the pool results follow expectations, England could face hosts Australia or Japan in Sydney on 31 October.

Australia would represent a serious challenge, particularly with a passionate home crowd behind them.

Japan, meanwhile, have already shown they can upset rugby's biggest nations.

England could reach the semi-finals without facing South Africa, New Zealand or France.

That's a pretty decent position to be in.

Get through the quarter-final and England could find Ireland or Argentina waiting in Sydney on 6 November.

Ireland will be desperate to finally break their World Cup quarter-final curse, while Argentina have repeatedly proved they can trouble the world's best.

Borthwick's men would need to produce something special.

But reaching the last four without facing one of the tournament's three traditional heavyweights would represent a huge opportunity.

And then comes the biggest challenge of all.

Defending champions South Africa, three-time winners New Zealand or France could be waiting in Sydney on 13 November.

The opposite half of the projected draw could even produce a blockbuster quarter-final between the Springboks and All Blacks.

As RUCK's full breakdown of every nation's World Cup route explains, England could benefit from their biggest rivals eliminating one another.

Of course, the actual knockout opponents will depend on pool results.

These are projected opponents based on expected pool finishes, not confirmed knockout fixtures.

title: Dragons cite 'dangerous' incident as Wales players hurt in derby
article_text:
Here are your rugby morning headlines for Sunday, October 25.

Dragons head coach Filo Tiatia bemoaned a "dangerous" knee-drop tackle that left centre Fetuli Paea limping off during their defeat to the Ospreys at St Helen's.

As well as Paea, the Dragons lost Wales internationals Rio Dyer and Ben Carter to injury - while they had Rhodri Williams, Tinus de Beer and Aneurin Owen all sin-binned.

Knee-drop tackles will be banned throughout rugby from November 1 after a recent World Rugby announcement.

"I saw the clip," said Tiatia about Paea's injury. "It was a knee-drop tackle.

"I know the law comes in in a couple of weeks. But you can clearly see it's dangerous.

"Rugby league is heavy on it. I think World Rugby need to bring it in earlier. But he's not good."

On Dyer, Tiatia admitted he didn't "know the extent of it".

"There's a few (injuries). The injuries, you saw Carts go off. We had three yellow cards through indiscipline. That's something we need to tighten up.

"The boys have been squeaky clean. Some of the things I saw differently. We've got a few clips for Mr Whitehouse so we can learn from them."

Scarlets head coach Nigel Davies believes his side have turned a corner after pushing the Stormers all the way in a thrilling BKT United Rugby Championship try fest in Cape Town.

Davies was left frustrated after Scarlets scored six tries but narrowly missed out on victory, insisting his players will take huge confidence and belief from a performance that proved they can compete with the best teams in the competition.

Scarlets had been written off before the match against the South African outfit, but they produced a spirited display to take the contest down to the wire and claim a try bonus point in a 52-40 defeat.

Davies was delighted with the way his players executed their attacking game plan under pressure, although he admitted there were key moments and costly inaccuracies that ultimately proved decisive.

"First of all, congratulations to the Stormers for winning what was a fantastic contest. We came here with an intent to score tries and play rugby. It has been our focus all season and we knew we were coming to a very difficult place to play and we had to be on top of our game.

"What we have been working on mentally, physically and skill-wise is to execute under high pressure and a higher intensity so we can compete longer against the top teams and I firmly believe we have turned the corner there. There is a belief within the squad that they can do that and the boys did that today.

"I was delighted for them for the respect they would have gained from a lot of people because of that performance and also the confidence that will grow within the group as well.

"I am delighted with that performance and absolutely disappointed because we could have potentially won it. There were a couple of key moments that didn’t go our way. We also put a bit of pressure on ourselves with our inaccuracies – something we have to look at, but it was a match that could have gone either way in the end."

Davies also highlighted the value of the experience for his younger players, singling out 18-year-old fly-half Carwyn Leggatt-Jones after the young playmaker was thrust into the challenge of facing the Stormers away from home.

"This is a fabulous place to play and a lot of my players would have gained a huge amount. Look at our 10, Carwyn Leggatt-Jones, who is just 18 years old, that experience will be invaluable to him.

"We had to make a few changes because of international calls, but I was confident with the depth in the squad and a lot of these boys have been unlucky not to play earlier. I was delighted with the way they stepped up."

Bristol Bears director of rugby Pat Lam admitted he was “really proud” of his team after they weathered the awful conditions and a second-half fightback from Exeter Chiefs to triumph 20-7 at Ashton Gate.

Gabriel Ibitoye crossed after 27 minutes to put the home side ahead, with James Williams adding the extras followed by a penalty on the half hour to establish a 10-0 lead.

Greg Fisilau’s try, converted by Henry Slade, then brought Exeter right back into contention, but a second Williams penalty gave Bristol some breathing space before Luka Ivanishvili touched down in the dying seconds to make sure of the win.

Heavy rain and strong winds made life difficult for both sides, and Lam said: “Conditions like that really challenge your technique and mindset.

“And you can’t go into these games without the right mindset because you have to front up physically, but that physicality has to be technically accurate, otherwise you are going to give territory and possession away and miss tackles.

“We allowed them back into the game by dropping a few balls, but our message was ‘just be accurate’.

“A lot of what we saw today was a result of the work we have done in pre-season, it was not a day to throw the ball around.”

Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter gently questioned his side’s decision not to go for the posts near the end to level the scores, instead turning down two kickable penalties inside the 22.

title: Pay war threatens to get ugly as deadline looms
article_text:
It’s been mostly fought out behind closed doors so far, but standby for the pay dispute between Australia’s professional players and Rugby Australia to go public – and get ugly – this week, with the deadline for a new collective bargaining agreement only days away.

And if you want to know what might unfold if the tense negotiations can’t produce a deal, the playbook of NRL players in their bitter CBA dispute in 2023 is a good reference point.

The Rugby Union Players’ Association (RUPA) and Rugby Australia have been at the table for months trying to strike a deal for a new five-year CBA, with the current agreement expiring on Saturday, October 31.

Based on dispatches from both trenches, it’s fair to say the talks have grown tetchy and relations have strained.

RUPA is pushing for a significant pay increase for men’s and women’s players, arguing the game needs to invest way more to generate success and reignite the game in Australia. It has also argued players should get a cut of the $100m fee coming to RA for co-hosting the men’s World Cup next year.

RA says it’s put up a good offer, with an uplift in minimum spend on players, and in bonuses for World Cup success.

RA argues it has a responsibility to not squander the big Lions and World Cup windfalls, and to use the money to secure the long-term future of the game in Australia. Some at RA were stunned at the size of RUPA’s initial pay demands.

Both sides have given ground and there is hope a deal can still be reached this week. But there are still some significant sticking points and much more ground-giving will likely be needed.

The stink between RUPA and RA comes after much smoother CBA deals in 2020 and 2022, when the game was under existential financial threat due to COVID.

But now the game is back on its feet, the players’ union has adopted a more combative stance and there’s a clear rugby league flavour to the RUPA camp.

New RUPA boss Adrian Turner, who took over in April, was formerly the head of legal at the Rugby League Players Association and he brought in another long-time RLPA figure, former Roosters and Manly player Tom Symonds, to become RUPA chief operating officer.

What happens if a deal can’t be reached by Saturday? A strike by the Wallabies or the Aussie sevens players is not on the cards, given players are under contract. But with no CBA in place, other action could be taken to put pressure on RA, such as refusing to participate in RA’s commercial events and wearing protest shirts at training.

In 2023, when the RLPA and the NRL couldn’t be reach a CBA deal by deadline, NRL stars then refused to do interviews with host broadcasters on match days, delayed kick-off times and even taped over the NRL logo on their jerseys. There were threats to repeat their pay dispute boycott of the 2003 Dally M Awards, but that didn’t eventuate, with a deal finally struck after a month-long, mid-season standoff.

The John Eales Medal night will be held on Friday – a night before the CBA deadline expires – so a boycott of that won’t happen either. Some other NRL’s squeeze points may also not translate to rugby, with players either playing overseas or just starting pre-season training. The Wallabies fly out for a spring tour to London on Saturday.

However it plays out, a public stoush about money will likely take skin off, for both sides. The clock ticks.

Australia A had more than enough power to overwhelm a disappointing USA side in Nashville on Sunday, overcoming a red card to cruise to a 61-12 victory.

With only a week’s training in “Music City”, Australia’s second XV stuck to playing pretty basic chords but dominance at set-piece and in the contact zones was enough to run up a score. David Feliuai was sent off for a high shot in the opening half, but it barely affected the Stephen Larkham-coached side.

The Aussie A back row were strong, with No.8 Joe Brial winning man of the match, and Will Harris and Rory Scott both busy. Nick Frost also turned in a good 80-minute shift, as he tries to earn his way back into the Wallabies.

In that same boat, Dylan Pietsch scored twice and defended like a back-rower in the middle of the field. Force halfback and former Highlander Nathan Hastie added to the growing list of Wallaby contenders at No.9, with a classy effort.

The sides will go at it again on Saturday in New Jersey, where the likes of Zac Lomax, Corey Toole and Luke Reimer will all likely get a start.

The Wallaroos finished the year with a third straight win over Scotland on Friday night in Canberra, and further highlighted some positive shifts already made under the new Tim Walsh regime.

Skills look sharper, and so too the Wallaroos’ ability to retain the ball and build pressure. The tendency to drop out of games for a 10-15 minute stretch is still a big work-on for Walsh, however.

The big takeaways of 2026? The impressive young halves partnership of Samantha Wood (22) and Waiaria Ellis (19) only gets better and better, and throw in Faitala Moleka (21) at No.12, and you have a long-term trio to take to the 2029 World Cup.

title: The Prem: Bristol 20-7 Exeter: Bears overcome Chiefs in tough conditions
article_text:
Bristol moved up to third place in the Prem after beating Exeter 20-7 at Ashton Gate.

Gabriel Ibitoye's 26th-minute try and James Williams' penalty three minutes later were the only scores of an attritional first half in difficult conditions.

Greg Fisilau was mauled over 12 minutes after the restart as Exeter got on the scoreboard.

The Chiefs tried to force a second, but it was Bristol that earned the win when Williams kicked an excellent 41-metre penalty before Luca Ivanishvili crashed over from close range after Olly Woodburn had fumbled a high ball.

His late try denied Exeter a losing bonus point and leaves Rob Baxter's side in ninth place on eight points, six behind the Bears.

The stormy weather's impact was in evidence from the first whistle as both sides struggled to keep hold of the ball.

Bristol almost scored in the opening 60 seconds after an Exeter mistake under a kick saw the ball bobble around in their in-goal area.

It was as close as either side came to scoring in the opening 26 minutes as the hosts had the better of the possession and territory but were stifled by a spirited Exeter defence.

The pressure finally told when Ibitoye got on the end of a looping Harry Randall pass and beat Zack Wimbush to dive into the left corner.

Williams' penalty soon after extended the lead to 10 points and Exeter then had Australia star Tom Hooper forced off with a shoulder injury just before the interval.

Despite that setback, Henry Slade almost dotted down a Sam Wolstenholme grubber kick four minutes after the restart before Exeter's maul got them back into the game soon after.

First the pack earned themselves a penalty and the second maul from the resulting lineout 10 metres out saw Fisilau forced over.

The Chiefs forwards won another penalty inside the 22 with eight minutes left, but superb work from Ibitoye saw the Bears turn the ball over six metres out.

Bristol went straight up the field and a penalty resulting from a high tackle was dispatched well by Williams despite the tough conditions.

And the weather proved to be a distraction for Woodburn soon after as he missed a high kick and was put under pressure by Ibitoye, who was stopped inches from the Exeter line.

But eight phases later Georgian replacement Ivanishvili forced his way over to seal a hard-fought victory.

"I'm really proud of the boys. We did what we needed to do to win, I felt.

"Some might say it's not pretty, but it's the type of rugby that needed to be played in these conditions.

"We knew earlier in the week it was going to be like this, so we just shone the light on this part of the game that we don't always use.

"This was the part of the game that we had to use, so I'm really pleased the boys got their rewards for it."

"I thought towards the end there we'd worked our way back into it and we had an opportunity to get something, didn't we?

"Obviously our poorest maul of the game probably was at the end point there when you probably needed to have a real killer maul at that stage.

"We weren't quite as good as we needed to be there, so we have to play away from it and then we lost the ball and then I think really that last period was the kind of errors you just can't afford to have in these conditions - not just handling errors but we gave away penalty error as well which gives a shot at goal.

"We did just make more errors than them over the course of today and tactically they were potentially a little smarter."

title: 6 big names who have just lost their DP World Tour card
article_text:
And just like that another DP World Tour campaign is done and dusted for everyone except the top 70.

While they will move onto the season-ending Playoffs to determine who will win the Race to Dubai and who will earn a PGA Tour card for next year, a number of players are facing the prospect of a daunting trip to Q School next month or at least one year relying on invites.

Who finished in the top 100 of the Race to Dubai Rankings?

Which big names lost their DP World Tour card?

With ongoing injury problems, Pepperell decided to skip the regular season-finale.

He had started the week just inside the mark after making important cuts in Spain and India, but the ever-popular Englishman was overtaken by Sean Crocker – and how. The American made the cut on the number before going on to post weekend rounds of 69-68. But that only tells half the story. Crocker went out in 39 on Sunday and looked like he would just fall short, but something clicked after the turn and he came home in just 29 shots to finish in a tie for 34th and leapfrog Pepperell.

Pepperell has taken it in good spirits though. “Now, Sean Crocker, that is how you do it,” he posted on X. “Big balls, minerals you could say. Very well done. You can buy me a bourbon when I next see you.”

The much-loved Thai player has overcome the Q School grind before, and he will need to go and do it again if he is to have playing rights next year.

The four-time DP World Tour winner was visibly emotional after he was forced to withdraw from the Genesis Championship as the toll of playing 11 straight weeks became too much for the 37-year-old.

Fisher celebrated his 500th DP World Tour start at the beginning of the season but now faces a difficult task to prolong his epic run. A Ryder Cup winner in 2010, Fisher has not won a tour event since the Tshwane Open 12 years ago. He is playing this season on a Career Money List exemption and will need to head to Q School to secure another year at Europe’s top table after a missed cut in Korea.

Another wily veteran, Siem was making his 594th appearance on the DP World Tour this week. He has had brief periods away from the circuit and had to progress through Q School in 2023. And the 46-year-old will be required to do the same again after he withdrew from the Genesis Championship following an opening-round 82.

The fiery Spaniard has had a torrid time this season, including a nun of nine straight cuts, and he won’t play the weekend in Korea either. That will mark the end of a 19-year stay at Europe’s top table for Larrazabal, who needed a runner-up finish this week to stand a chance of making it to 20.

“Well very, very, very tough,” he said when asked to reflect on his week. “Yeah, just a very tough moment. I had to play my worst golf the season that I had to keep my card.”

Larrazabal has struggled to get over a missed putt to win the Bahrain Championship in 2025. “It’s been a tough 20 months,” the nine-time DP World Tour winner, who will now head to Q School, said. “What changed it all was throwing out the 10th victory in Bahrain last year. Not making the putt on the last to win was very tough. It took me a while to go through that one.

“This year has been tough. I’m very tired. As I said, I played nine of the last 10 weeks. and I have to recover my old body to try to play six good rounds in Infinitum and to try to keep the dream alive.”

Another player whose winner’s exemption runs out at the end of the season, Smylie earned just north of $8 million on LIV Golf this year.

While he has yet to publicly state whether or not he will stay with the league, the Australian will need to head to Q School if he wants to have a DP World Tour card in 2027 after missing the cut in Korea.

title: Talking points: USA make it five straight Test wins with emphatic Italy victory
article_text:
The USA Women’s Eagles beat Italy 54–24 in Nashville to register their fifth Test victory in a row.

It was an astonishingly brutal performance from Jack Hanratty’s side, who went 12-0 down in the opening 15 minutes as Francesca Granzotto and Francesca Sgorbini dotted down in the early exchanges.

Soon enough, the Eagles took commanding control of the fixture. By half-time, Keia Mae Sagapolu-Sanele had dotted down twice, while Lauryn Carlton and Freda Tafuna had crossed the whitewash once each. Bella Vogel was spotless off the kicking tee.

The second half was a little more competitive, but the game had been comfortably won by the time Zoë Naude blew the final whistle.

In that second 40 minutes, Tafuna scored two more tries to secure her second WXV Global Series hat-trick. Georgie Perris-Redding scored her fourth try in two games, and Kate Zackary added some extra gloss to the scoreboard.

The Italians did see team veterans Vittoria Ostuni Minuzzi and Beatrice Rigoni dot down before full-time. Those scores counted for relatively little in the end, and Plinio Sciamanna’s team finished the WXV Global Series with one win from four matches.

After a difficult opening 15 minutes in Tennessee, during which the USA watched Italy’s Francesca Granzotto and Francesca Sgorbini cross the try line, the Eagles went back to what they do best: using pure power.

All of their tries on Saturday came from forwards. Keia Mae Sagapolu-Sanele went over twice after the hosts worked through the phases in Italy’s 22. Soon enough, debutant Lauryn Carlton crossed the try line too. The former college hammer thrower received a pop pass from Freda Tafuna and burrowed over from close range.

Tafuna had already delivered several strong carries before sending Carlton over the whitewash. She then scored a try of her own just before half-time as Italy failed to stop her from rumbling over the line.

The ability to revert to such a devastating, forward-dominated style was hugely impressive. Italy had absolutely no answer for it.

When the second half got underway, it was much the same. Three minutes after the restart, Tafuna scored her second try from close range. The back-row forward completed her hat-trick shortly after Georgie Perris-Redding crossed the line too. Kate Zackary’s 76th-minute score further underlined the USA’s forward dominance.

It felt like we had seen this Italy performance before. The opening 40 minutes were a perfect example. They had bright moments but could not maintain their attacking momentum.

Granzotto’s try was absolutely astonishing. The speed with which Italy decided to pull the trigger, and Emma Stevanin’s execution of a cross-field kick to the wing, were exceptional. Sgorbini’s reading of the USA’s exit and her subsequent charge-down were also excellent examples of rugby nous.

But almost immediately after the second try, Italy’s momentum ran out. The Eagles dominated from that point onwards.

Italy’s attacking forays were either snuffed out by the USA defence or squandered. The Eagles’ forwards were in their element.

Plinio Sciamanna must find a way for the Azzurre to maintain their momentum. Without that, we could see this extremely talented group of players go backwards.

Of course, there was more wrong with Italy’s performance than just that. Their scrum was dominated, and their tackle completion rate stood at 80% when the final whistle blew.

It was not all negative. A more pragmatic approach helped Vittoria Ostuni Minuzzi cross the whitewash in the 55th minute. By full-time, Beatrice Rigoni had done the same. It just was not enough.

Italy now face a long wait before returning to action against France in the 2027 Guinness Women’s Six Nations. There is work to be done.

Perhaps the most impressive part of the USA Women’s Eagles’ first year under Jack Hanratty has been his ability to identify new talent.

It quickly became clear that 19-year-old Bella Vogel was ready to start at Test level. A couple of months later, Nina Mason emerged as another promising prospect. Abigail Paton gave up the dream of playing for the Black Ferns to become an Eagle. Hanratty has also worked well with the Women’s Sevens head coach to integrate several players from the HSBC SVNS Series squad into Test rugby.

Lauryn Carlton was the latest debutant for the team on Saturday. Stepping into the shoes of Hope Rogers is no easy task, but the Boston Banshees loosehead prop rose to the challenge. She is another player to keep an eye on.

The idea that the USA have been a sleeping giant has never seemed more applicable than it does this year. This crop of young, exciting players coming through the ranks has put the Eagles on an entirely different plane.

With an out-of-sorts England team coming to New Jersey next week, the prospect of the USA pulling off an upset is not beyond the realms of possibility. All eyes will be on Sports Illustrated Stadium.

title: Ospreys thump Dragons on return to St Helen's
article_text:
Ospreys enjoyed a happy homecoming with a bonus-point victory over Dragons at St Helen's.

Mark Jones' side returned to the famous Swansea venue in style, scoring five tries in horrendous conditions in front of 5,592 supporters.

Ospreys led 19-7 at half-time after a double by Reuben Morgan-Williams and an effort by captain Sam Parry.

Dragons scored with the final play of the half through Rio Dyer, but Ospreys' driving line-out secured the win by earning a penalty try and a score for Ross Moriarty.

Anzelo Tuitavuki went over for the visitors' second, but they endured an evening to forget.

Dragons had Rhodri Williams, Tinus de Beer and Aneurin Owen sin-binned and Wales were also given a scare before the Nations Championship.

Dyer did not come out for the second half and lock Ben Carter, who established himself in Steve Tandy's starting line-up last season, went off with a head injury.

After some pre-match pomp, Ospreys started strongly and got their reward when scrum-half Morgan-Williams burrowed over from close range in the sixth minute, Dan Edwards adding the extras.

The visitors did a good job of playing into the wind and had been the better side, but then conceded a scrappy second on the half hour.

Morgan-Williams was the beneficiary of Dragons' failure to fall on the ball after a grubber through by centre Lalakai Foketi.

Ospreys were over for a third time as half-time approached when fly-half Edwards was brave with a penalty touch-finder and the pack muscled over from a five-metre driving line-out for Parry's score.

A 19-0 lead would have represented a good effort for Ospreys with the wind, but Dragons had the final say of the half when, after pressure and penalties, recalled Wales wing Dyer crossed for his first try of the season.

Those seven points were cancelled out almost straight from the restart when Ospreys were awarded a penalty try for a 20-metre line-out drive being stopped illegally, with scrum-half Rhodri Williams sin-binned.

Dragons then suffered the loss of co-captain Carter and, straight after Williams' return, a yellow card for De Beer.

Edwards pinned them into the corner from the resulting penalty and the pack did the rest, back-row forward Moriarty following Parry in scoring against his former side.

Tuitavuki gave Dragons a smidgen of hope when he sniped at a ruck and powered over with quarter of an hour left, but that was soon followed by Owen's yellow card for a head-on-head tackle.

After a first block of the season that has seen Ospreys play in Durban, Johannesburg, Tbilisi and Newport, they returned to the famous sporting venue they left in 2005.

They have downsized after leaving the Swansea.com Stadium in 2025 and, while there is a long snagging list and plenty of jobs to be done, this felt like a home.

Like at Bridgend's Brewery Field, their ground for 2025-26, there was a lively atmosphere to make up for the rough edges.

It was Ospreys' first game at St Helen's since moving a game against Benetton during the Covid pandemic in 2020.

Their return meant there were plenty of smiles despite torrential rain, especially from the punter who conquered the conditions to win a new £20,000 bathroom by passing the ball through a hole at half-time.

Ospreys came out firing after the restart to ensure that their first half efforts did not go down the pan on a night to remember for the region as they continue to fight for their existence.

title: Glasgow recover 17-point deficit to beat Benetton
article_text:
Glasgow recovered from 17 points down to win a thriller at Benetton and continue their unbeaten start to the United Rugby Championship season.

The visitors went into half-time 10-0 down after a disappointing first-half display.

They squandered several attacking opportunities and were scythed open by Benetton fly-half Jacob Umaga, who released centre Federico Zanandrea for the game's first try.

Umaga also kicked a penalty before the break and when Louis Lynagh intercepted Matthew Urwin's pass to score under the posts on 42 minutes, Benetton appeared to be cruising to victory.

However, Glasgow responded in fine style, scoring three tries in eight minutes to level the scores.

Euan Ferrie went over off the back of a trademark rolling maul, captain Kyle Steyn crossed in the corner after some good hands and Rory Darge finished off a sweeping team move started by Steyn.

Umaga nudged Benetton back into the lead off the tee, but with time running out, lock Jare Oguntibeju crashed over from close range for Glasgow's fourth try.

It proved to be the decisive blow as Franco Smith's side navigated the final moments for a hard-fought win.

Warriors are second in the URC table, behind Edinburgh, after three wins and a draw, while Benetton sit 15th.

title: Scarlets denied by Stormers in 14-try thriller
article_text:
Centre Joe Roberts scored a hat-trick but Scarlets suffered defeat by Stormers in a remarkable 14-try United Rugby Championship (URC) contest.

A late double by Yaqeen Ahmed sealed victory for the South Africans leaving Scarlets with just a try bonus despite having shot at a famous win at 40-40.

Unlike the UK weather, the perfect conditions for running rugby in Cape Town led to a thrilling encounter in which both sides traded blows.

Stormers led 33-14 at half-time and a try bonus through Zachary Porthen, Hasseim Pead, Ntuthuko Mchunu, Seabelo Senatla and Deon Fourie.

More efforts followed by Olly Reid and Ahmed but Scarlets showed fighting spirit and attacking flair.

Wales centre Roberts went over three times along with Ioan Jones, Josh Macleod and Macs Page, who was helped from the field after a heavy head injury.

Scarlets, who have never beaten Stormers, scrapped their way to 40-40 in the final quarter but failed to make it a hat-trick of wins after beating Benetton and Newcastle.

They now finish the first block of the season with an equally daunting fixture against Bulls in Pretoria next weekend.

Nigel Davies' side will need to drastically improve their defence and set-piece to stand a chance of upsetting the odd at Loftus Versfeld.

Scarlets were chasing the game from early on after John Dobson's side struck twice when hooker John McKee was yellow-carded for cynically killing the ball in the 11th minute.

Tight-head prop Porthen went over from a cunning line-out move followed by a much more dashing second, scrum-half Pead crossing from a sensational Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu offload behind his back.

The 14-man Scarlets responded well with Roberts, who missed out on Wales' Nations Championship squad, put over down the right by wing Jones.

But that was cancelled out by rampaging loose-head Ntuthuko Mchunu powering over from loose line-out ball.

After providing an assist for the first, Jones finished magnificently down the right for Scarlets' second but once again Stormers hit straight back.

Wing Senatla and hooker Fourie scored either side of a second Jones effort being chalked off for a forward pass for a commanding 33-14 lead.

It seemed Scarlets were already playing for a consolation bonus in a heavy loss, yet it was game on thanks to a pair of quickfire tries after the restart.

A searing break by full-back Ioan Nicholas led to in-form wing Page going over and then Roberts intercepted for the four-try bonus.

Page was then helped from the field with an oxygen mask after hitting his head heavily on the ground as he attempted to score.

Stormers turned to their tight game to regain control, earning penalties to march down the field for prop Reid to score.

Scarlets would not go away and drew level through Macleod and Roberts while the abscence of a Stormers hooker meant uncontested scrums.

Yet the hosts got their noses back in front in the 73rd minute when Ahmed was worked under the posts before he took away a Scarlets' bonus with a late breakaway.

title: Resurgent Tigers overpower Saints in derby downpour
article_text:
Leicester Tigers gained revenge for their defeat in last season's Prem playoff semi-finals to defeat rivals Northampton Saints in torrential conditions at Mattioli Woods Welford Road.

In a first half played at the mercy of the weather, neither team was able to find a rhythm, with James Pater's early opportunist try and Freddie Steward's long-range penalty the only scores on the board.

But, inspired by a major scuffle on the verge of half-time, the Tigers subsequently dominated.

First, Jamie Blamire drove over from a rolling maul, before Cam Henderson barrelled his way through Saints tacklers to slide over in the corner.

Faced with the onslaught, the shellshocked Saints were unable to prevent further tries from Finn Carnduff and Steward, as the visitors' wait for a league win at their near rivals stretches to four years.

With the rain teeming down it was Saints who struck first. Playing with an advantage, Fin Smith's speculative kick ahead was spilled by Billy Searle allowing Pater to gather and score.

As the penalty count escalated amid the squall, neither team was able to keep the ball for long, but Freddie Steward gave the home fans something to shout about with a well judged penalty from 50 metres out.

Neither team was able to rely on their lineout, with Blamire suffering particularly at the hands of the marauding Josh Kemeny.

But with the whistle blown for half-time, the game's momentum shifted. A major scuffle involving multiple players broke out on the touchline, which eventually led to Ollie Chessum pushing England team-mate Henry Pollock down the tunnel.

Seemingly inspired by the tussle, the Tigers came out with a renewed purpose after the break.

Within minutes, Blamire was able to find his jumper five metres out and with the backs adding their weight, the Tigers powered over. The hooker ultimately emerging with the ball.

Having attained dominance in the scrum, the Tigers then struck again. Following strong running from Solomone Kata, Gabe Hamer-Webb and Henderson combined down the wing, to send the lock over the whitewash.

The Tigers were in the ascendancy and soon had a third through Carnduff, who drove over after a short-range pass from the imperious Joe Heyes as the Saints' defence tired.

Steward then put the gloss on the victory. The full-back stepping Archie McParland to grab what had appeared an unlikely try bonus point, to the delight of the home fans.

The result leaves the Tigers in second behind Gloucester, while Northampton drop to fourth.

"I thought the players really took hold of [the game] in the second half. Some of the guys in the pack, the way we worked physically for each other – I'm really pleased.

"The set-piece didn't function early on. We were slow to adapt to the officiating there, but we got on the front foot and showed our power and application in that side of the game.

"The way that the players problem-solved at the set piece, which was an issue early, was brilliant and I'm just really pleased with the emotional energy that they threw into that game."

"The changing room was honestly the calmest dressing room you could think of. We didn't have lots of tactical messages, we just felt we needed to be a bit more accurate and we'd gain the ascendancy."

"[In the second half] we didn't control that kicking game as well we had been. At the set piece the penalty count was very high – we didn't manage to produce enough ball, create enough pressure and we gave them lots of opportunities to score in our 22.

"They had the momentum throughout the second-half, our actions were neither accurate or aggressive enough and its cost us."

"A very bitter pill with that second half performance in particular."

"We play a winter sport and we have to get over that. We didn't work it out today and we need to be better at it [playing in the wet].

title: Ulster still without URC win after defeat by Bulls
article_text:
Ulster's winless start to the United Rugby Championship stretched to four games as they were beaten 34-26 by the Bulls in Pretoria.

Former Ulster star Marcell Coetzee led the way for his side in a dominant pack effort, scoring two tries despite spending 10 minutes in the sin-bin.

From 21-0 down, the northern province did at least mount something of a comeback to secure a four-try bonus, although they were denied further consolation with Curwin Bosch's last-kick penalty knocking them out of losing bonus-point range.

While Richie Murphy's side did notch a Challenge Cup win against Zebre last week, it is the first time they have failed to win any of their first four league fixtures since 2008-09 when they opened what was then the Celtic League with a quartet of consecutive losses.

They face a second game in South Africa against Stormers on 31 October before the URC takes a four-weekend break for November's Nations Championship fixtures.

In what was a clumsy start, Ulster conceded a penalty in the opening passage of play and were quickly made to pay when Coetzee finished off a maul try after only two minutes.

Turned over when given the opportunity to respond in kind, Ulster were soon defending their own line again but it took until the 19th minute for the Bulls to double their advantage, the hosts opting for the quick-tap when five metres out to set up an infield maul with Elrigh Louw dotting down.

With both the altitude and the bruising nature of the contest taking its toll on Ulster, Coetzee was over for his second and his side's third with a pick-and-go from close range eight minutes before the interval.

Seemingly hanging on and no more in the contest, Ulster scored their first points of the half with the clock in the red after working the ball well through the hands to send the speedy Chay Mullins over in the corner for his second try of the season.

Despite an uneven start to the campaign that now comprises of two draws and two losses in the league, spirited second halves have been a story of Ulster's season and they again were much brighter after the restart.

Mike Lowry thought he was over only to run out of room in the left corner but flanker David McCann barged across soon after.

Having been rocking on their heels in the first half, Jack Murphy's second conversion of the day left just seven points in it and Ulster's prospects improved further with Coetzee sent to the sin-bin after being shown a yellow card that stayed yellow when reviewed by the TMO bunker for a high hit.

By the time the former Springbok returned, it was his side who had scored the only points of his absence through a Handre Pollard penalty.

It was a further 10 minutes after the Bulls' captain's reintroduction before the game's next score with Keynan Knox doing well to create space for his team-mates to send Mullins over for his second.

Deflatingly for the visitors, virtually from the restart Johan Grobbelaar scored yet another forwards' try for the Bulls.

Stuart McCloskey, one of eight Ulster players who featured now joining up with Ireland for the Nations Championship, set up a grandstand finish with his side's fourth try 10 minutes from time.

They could not, however, close the gap in the final stages before Bosch's concluding penalty cost them a further point.

title: Katerina Siniakova and Ashlyn Krueger ranking points and prize money after Japan Open final
article_text:
Japan Open title winner Katerina Siniakova and runner-up Ashlyn Krueger are both set to return to the top 50 of the rankings following their impressive performances in Tokyo.

Both finalists were unseeded and beat seeds en route to the final with Siniakova defeating second seed Peyton Stearns and eighth seed Katie Boulter to reach her 11 WTA Tour singles final while Krueger beat sixth seed Janice Tjen, fourth seed Talia Gibson and top seed Ann Li.

After needing more than two hours and three sets to get the better of Li, Krueger – who won the tournament in 2023 – never really got going in the final as Siniakova ran away with the match and the title with the Czech winning 6-1, 6-0 in one hour and eight minutes to secure her sixth WTA singles trophy.

Doubles great Siniakova broke in games one, five and seven of the opening set and ended up winning 10 consecutive games with further breaks in games three, four and six of the second set.

For Siniakova, it is a first singles title since she won the Jiangxi Open three years ago while the 2023 Japan Open remains Krueger’s only top-level trophy to date.

And while Siniakova has won “only” six singles titles, she is one of the all-time great doubles players as she has won 39 women’s doubles trophies with seven of those coming in 2026.

The 30-year-old has also completed two Career Grand Slams as she has won the Australian Open three times, the French Open four times, Wimbledon three times and the US Open twice.

But both have received handy boosts in the WTA Rankings with their performances at the WTA 250 tournament.

Siniakova, who has peaked at No 27 in the singles rankings, started the tournament at No 86 and she has surged 37 places to No 49 in the Live WTA Rankings after picking up 249 points.

Former world No 29 Krueger kicked off her Japan Open campaign at No 55 and she earned 163 points, resulting in an 11-place jump to No 44.

Siniakova’s 2026 earnings were $3,293,819 before the start of the Japan Open with most of that coming from doubles as she won the French Open and US Open women’s doubles events while her career total was $18,238,169.

She will add another $37,390 to those totals for winning the WTA 250 event.

Krueger, who had earned $1,351,128 in 2026 and 44,228,657 over her career, collects a cheque of $22,125 for finishing runner-up.

title: Klugman to face Jacquemot in Wrexham Open final
article_text:
British teenager Hannah Klugman will face France's Elsa Jacquemot in Sunday's Lexus Wrexham Open singles final.

Klugman, 17, won her semi-final 6-1, 6-4 against compatriot Jodie Burrage, to reach what will be the biggest match of her career.

She will face Jacquemot who overcame the Netherlands' Suzan Lamens 6-2, 7-6 to earn her spot in the final.

However, Klugman's hopes of appearing in both the singles and doubles finals were ended after losing the semi-final alongside partner Daniella Britton to fellow Brits Freya Christie and Eden Silva 7-6 6-4.

title: Popov is back in the French Open final!
article_text:
The YONEX French Open 2026 semifinals delivered an exciting day in Paris, with Christo Popov keeping French hopes alive after two heartbreaking defeats for the home favourites.

Christo Popov produced an outstanding performance against China's Hu Zhe An, winning 21-14, 21-10 to reach his second consecutive French Open final.

"I think every point was kind of a match in my head," Popov explained after the victory.

Having lost last year's final, the Frenchman now has another opportunity to claim the title on home soil.

"I think fun is on the way. I'm gonna enjoy a lot tomorrow, and I'm gonna share it with the crowd."

Alex Lanier's impressive winning streak came to an end against Indonesia's 19-year-old Moh. Zaki Ubaidillah, who won 21-16, 16-21, 21-17 to reach his first Super 750 final.

"I'm definitely proud of myself," Lanier said, despite admitting frustration with his performance.

There was also disappointment for world champions Thom Gicquel/Delphine Delrue, who lost a thrilling three-game semifinal to China's Feng Yan Zhe/Huang Dong Ping, 21-19, 17-21, 19-21.

A red card for delaying play during the closing stages at 19-19 in the third game left the French pair frustrated.

"It's really frustrating to end a match like this," they said afterwards.

Elsewhere, An Se Young and P. V. Sindhu secured their places in the women's singles final, while Malaysia's Pearly Tan/Thinaah Muralitharan will face Japan's Yuki Fukushima/Mayu Matsumoto.

Malaysia also enjoyed a successful day in men's doubles, with both Man Wei Chong/Tee Kai Wun and Goh Sze Fei/Nur Izzuddin reaching Sunday's final.

All eyes now turn to Christo Popov, who will look to become the first French champion of the modern French Open when he faces Moh. Zaki Ubaidillah on Sunday.

The Korea Racing Authority signed an official sponsorship agreement with Gyeongju horse breeding organizations on the 18th to strengthen the prestige of the 'Breeders' Cup Rookie,' a representative domestic two-year-old horse racing event.

The Korea Racing Authority announced that it has concluded an official sponsorship agreement for the Breeders' Cup Rookie between the Korea Gyeongju Horse Breeders Association and the Korea Inland Horse Breeders Association, marking the beginning of efforts to promote Gyeongju horse breeding and strengthen the foundation for developing domestic horses.

The Breeders' Cup Rookie is the final race in the juvenile, or two-year-old, series, serving as a representative event to verify the abilities of domestic two-year-old Gyeongju horses and discover outstanding next-generation horses.

In particular, it is highly regarded by breeders, horse owners, trainers, and racing fans alike due to its ability to assess the growth potential of young Gyeongju horses at an early stage.

Under this agreement, the Korea Gyeongju Horse Breeders Association will participate as an official sponsor of the Breeders' Cup Rookie, providing a total sponsorship fund of 200 million won. The Korea Racing Authority will also invest a separate 100 million won as operating funds for auction vouchers, planning to run a production reinvestment program totaling 300 million won.

A representative from the Korea Racing Authority, speaking by phone with this outlet, stated, "The Breeders' Cup Rookie is a symbolic event that selects two-year-old horses who will lead the future of Korean horse racing."

French Open: Ubaidillah Bursts Lanier Bubble
article_text:
Moh. Zaki Ubaidillah kept the French crowd waiting for a home celebration, beating Alex Lanier in a gripping semifinal to reach his first Super 750 final.

Winning 21-16 16-21 21-17 against the world champion on home soil, Ubaidillah showed composure well beyond his 19 years. He was quick to the net, sharp and, above all, smooth and calm throughout.

“I’m very grateful to win. It was a very good match with Alex,” Ubaidillah told BWF. “I just tried to get into a good position and stay active.”

“My key was to attack more and play at the front of the net,” he explained. “From that area, I could get into a more attacking position.”

The breakthrough marks a major moment for 19-year-old, who said he could now enjoy the achievement while learning from it, after his Asian Games success.

“It’s a good moment for me,” he said. “Now I can enjoy it more after the Asian Games and learn more for the next tournament.”

There was pride, but no premature celebration. With the final still to come, his attention was already turning to the next challenge. “I’m very proud, of course, but I don’t want to celebrate early,” he said. “I still have another match and I want to win the title.”

Joining him in the final is another Frenchman, Christo Popov, who made his second home tournament back-to-back after showing Hu Zhe An the door 21-14 21-10. This will be their second meeting with Popov taking the first encounter.

Top seeds Feng Yan Zhe/Huang Dong Ping are through to a third consecutive final after gaining revenge on Thom Gicquel/Delphine Delrue in a gripping semifinal.

Just two months after falling to the French pair in the World Championships final, Feng and Huang turned the tables on home soil, overcoming the reigning world champions 19-21 21-17 21-19 in front of a packed Arena Grand Paris crowd.

“The games were really close to each other,” said Feng post match. “We encouraged each other, communicated and always focused on the match. The atmosphere was perfect,” he added. “The fans supported both sides and we also had Chinese supporters cheering for us. All players enjoy this kind of environment.”

The result not only avenged their defeat in August’s World Championships final but also kept alive their bid for a third consecutive title. Despite the pair’s good form, Huang insisted there would be no sense of entitlement heading into the final.

“Both sides start from the same place,” she said. “We just have to be ourselves while pursuing the win.”

There was also an unusual subplot to the semifinal. Having played earlier in the day Chen Fang Hui joined Feng/Huang’s coach in the coaching chair during the match, offering a different perspective. Huang explained that the decision was entirely spontaneous.

Chen, Huang revealed, had simply been passing by when they invited her to sit courtside. “We think it was a good choice. Chen did a good job.”

Awaiting them in the final are Hoo Pang Ron/Lai Pei Jing, who defeated Guo Xin Wa/Chen Fang Hui 21-13 21-9 earlier in the day.

title: Weather suspends Sunday's final round of Butterfield Bermuda Championship
article_text:
No play will occur Sunday at the Butterfield Bermuda Championship because of extreme weather conditions. More information regarding play on Monday will be provided no later than 4 p.m. ET., according to PGA Tour Communications on X.

Final-round action was scheduled to begin earlier than normal on Sunday in anticipation of the weather; however, play never began as wind gusts rose over 40 mph. After multiple delays, the PGA Tour Rules Committee called off play for the day. Conditions were expected to further deteriorate throughout the afternoon.

Seamus Power and Austin Smotherman were tied for the lead at 16-under after three rounds, two shots clear of Corey Conners, Taylor Moore and Ben Silverman.
